Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 1:

Surat at-Takwir

It is also said: "Surat Kuwwirat," and "Surat Idha ash-shamsu kuwwirat." It is Makki without any disagreement, and its verses number twenty-nine; in at-Taysir (the count is) twenty-eight. It contains a description of the state of the Day of Resurrection, which is what the end of the surah comprises, before what is in it.

Imam Ahmad and at-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he were seeing it with his own eye, let him recite ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ and ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾ and ﴿When the sky is split open﴾."

That is, the three surahs, and that is sufficient as a connection (between them).

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾: that is, "folded up," from "kawwartu al-'imamah" when you wind a turban. It is a metaphor for raising it and removing it from its place, by the relation of concomitance (lazum), for when a garment is to be lifted it is wrapped and folded and then lifted. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿The Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. It is also permissible that what is meant is the folding up of its light, which is spread out over the horizons and dispersed in the regions, either because "the sun" is a metaphor for "the light," as this is common in usage, or by supposing an omitted genitive (muda), or by a figurative extension in the attribution (ta'awwuz fi al-isnad), and what is meant by its folding is its removal, metaphorically, by the relation of concomitance, as you have just heard; or its lifting and concealing is a metaphor (isti'arah), as has been said. The comparison of light to jewels and to mental matters, which, when lifted, are folded in a garment, has been considered, and then the metaphor is regarded, and the "takwir" in the sense of "folding" is made a qarinah (indicator), so that there is a metaphor that is implicit and imaginative (isti'arah makniyyah takhyiliyyah). That what is meant is the removal of its light is related from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid, and it is the apparent meaning of what a group narrated from Ibn Abbas in his tafsir of ﴿kuwwirat﴾ as "became dark." The apparent meaning is that this occurs while its body remains, like the moon in its eclipse, and there are reports that support this. It has also been said that this is an expression for the removal of the sun's very essence and its taking away, because of the customary concomitance and the implication that the removal of the concomitant entails the removal of what it concomitates. It is also permissible that what is meant by ﴿kuwwirat﴾ is "it was cast out of its orbit and thrown down," from the verb "hawwara" and "kawwara," meaning: he threw it gathered onto the earth. Its being cast into Hell along with its worshippers, as some elevated reports indicate, and its light going away at that time, as al-Qurtubi stated explicitly, or into the sea, as indicated by the report of Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh from Ibn Ataik, in which Allah Most High sends a dabur wind which blows upon it, that is the sea, until it turns into fire. The great size of the body of the sun today does not necessitate the impossibility of its being cast into the sea on that day, since the state may differ between the two times, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is powerful over all things. However, sahih reports have come that "the sun will draw near to the heads on the Day of Resurrection in the place of gathering until it is about a mile away, and the sweat will bridle the people on that day," and the seas at that time will be thrown into it afterward, and they will not return. And from Abu Salih: "kuwwirat" means "nukkisat" (overturned). In another report from Ibn Abbas: its takwir is its being made to enter the Throne. And from Mujahid also: it was obliterated. The root of the form revolves around circling and gathering. This is all; and we have not found any of the early scholars holding that its folding is meant literally. Among the later scholars there is disagreement about whether that meaning is permissible. It has been said: it is not permissible to intend it, because the sun is a solid spherical body, and the ultimate sense of folding is circling, which is already present in it. It has been said: it is permissible, because the sun's being like that is not something the people of the science of description (ahl al-sharh) affirm; and even granting it, it is possible that a capacity for folding may come to exist in it, by His (glorified be He) making it spread out and then folding it, and for Him, Mighty and Majestic, in that are the wisdoms He has. What, in my view, makes the literal meaning unlikely is that it, whatever its state, is among the bodies that cannot be folded like garments. Yes, power at every time is not frustrated by anything. The raising of ﴿the sun﴾ is by a hidden verb that the mentioned one explains, according to the majority of the Basran grammarians, because the conditional "idha" is, in their view, specific to the verb; and it is by beginning (ibtida') according to al-Akhfash and the Kufans, since there is no such specificity in their view; and the supposition of an omitted element is contrary to the original.

And likewise is said regarding His saying, Most High:

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 81, verse 2:

﴿And when the stars fall, scattering﴾. That is, they fall and drop down, as ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Mujahid and Qatada. From the same root: *inkadara al-bāzī* means the falcon swooped down swiftly onto what it seizes. Al-ʿAjjaj, praising ʿUmar ibn ʿUmar al-Tamimi, said:

*When the noble men rush to the prize, the first to reach it is the one who wins.*
*He swoops as the falcon swoops, as the falcon dives down.*

*He drew his wings close to the mountain-slope and passed by,*
*and when he saw a flock of crows in the open, he swooped down.*

This is one of two reports from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also reported from him that he said: "On that day no star will remain without falling to the earth." And also from him: "The stars are lamps suspended between the sky and the earth by chains of light, in the hands of angels of light. When those in the heavens and the earth die, they will fall from the angels' hands." The apparent meaning of this is that the stars are not fixed in orbs (*aflak*) belonging to them, as the earlier philosophers say, but are suspended in space. In one respect this is close to the view of the later philosophers, who also hold that the stars are in space, but held by mutually attracting forces, not suspended by chains in the hands of angels. Beyond what is observed of them there is nothing but "sky" in the sense of a direction of height, not "sky" in its well-known sense. If the report of the rabbi (*ḥibr*) is sound, and it has the status of a report traced to the Prophet, we should not depart from its apparent meaning unless its impossibility becomes evident, and that is far-fetched. In that case the matter is easy. Some scholars who are qualified in this field have stated that the term "angels" may be applied to noble spiritual beings (*al-arbab al-nuriyya*), as in the report: "Indeed every thing has a king (*malik*), and with every drop of rain that falls there descends an angel."

And the report: *"There came to me the king of the mountains and the king of the seas."*

These are called the Platonic Forms (*al-muthul al-Aflatuniyya*, the ideas of Plato), and they are immaterial lights subsisting in themselves, governing the things that are nourished by the permission of God Most High. They preserve these things. They are the forces of growth, nourishment, and generation in plants and animals. It is said that by "the chains" is meant the powers by which the arrangements of things are preserved, or something similar.

It has also been said: "*inkadarat*" means "they became dim and their light was obliterated," as in the other report from Ibn ʿAbbas, from *kadartu al-māʾ fa-inkadar* (I made the water turbid, so it became turbid). In this there is a comparison between the extinguishing of their light and the clouding of water, which no longer keeps its clarity and the brightness of its appearance. In that case, according to some reports, they will be with their worshippers in the Fire. Clearly the stars do not include the sun. It has also been said that they do include it, and the mention of the sun after the stars is then a generalization after a specification. So do not be heedless.

When the mountains are set in motion. That is: they are removed from their places upon the earth through the quaking that occurs, on the basis that "setting in motion" is a metaphor for that. It was also said: they are set in motion after being lifted up into the air, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass﴾. And this happens only after the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah).

﴿Wa-idha al-ʿishār﴾ (And when the pregnant camels are neglected). *ʿishār* is the plural of *ʿushrāʾ*, like *nifās* is the plural of *nufasāʾ*. It refers to the she-camel that has passed ten months since the stallion was let loose on her, and this name continues to apply to her until she gives birth. It may also be applied to her after she has given birth, since she is then at her most precious to her people and their dearest possession.

﴿ʿUtțilat﴾ (are neglected): left unattended, with no herdsman and no one seeking them out. It is also said that their owners neglected them from milking and from tying their udders, and it is also said that they neglected letting the stallions mount them. This would be the case shortly before the Hour arrives, when their owners are preoccupied with what will overtake them at that time.

It is also said that this neglect will happen on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Qurtubi said: "The speech is figurative (*tamthīl*, allegorical depiction), since there will be no pregnant camels at that time. The meaning is that if there were pregnant camels, their owners would neglect them and busy themselves with themselves." It is also said that it is meant literally: that is, when they rise from their graves and see the wild beasts, the livestock and the animals gathered together, and see their pregnant camels, which were their noblest possessions, they will pay them no heed because of their preoccupation with themselves. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

It is also said that *al-ʿishār* means the clouds, likening a cloud that is expected to rain to a pregnant she-camel whose delivery is near. In this there is a subtle metaphor (*istiʿāra*), together with complete appropriateness between it and what precedes it, since clouds gather over the peaks of mountains and are seen there. Its being appropriate to what follows, according to the first view, does not conflict with this, since that is a literal meaning, preferred on its own merits. The neglect of them is a figurative expression (*majāz*) for the absence of anticipating their rain, because people are preoccupied with other matters.

It is also said that it means their failing to rain. It is also said that *al-diyār* (the dwellings) are meant, which are left neglected and are not inhabited. It is also said that the land whose crops are tithed is meant, which is left neglected and not cultivated.

Mudar al-Yazidi read *ʿuţilat* with a light pronunciation and the passive form. Al-Lawāmiḥ transmitted this from Ibn Kathir, then said: "This is an error; the reading is actually *ʿaṭalat* with two fatḥas, meaning *taʿaṭṭalat* (became neglected), because its doubled form (*ʿaṭṭala*) is transitive. It is said: *ʿaṭṭaltu al-shayʾ* and *aʿṭaltuhu*, so that *ʿaṭala* functions intransitively by itself, and *ʿaṭalat al-marʾa* (the woman became adorned with no jewelry) when she has no ornaments on her. Perhaps this reading is a dialect in which *faʿʿaltu* and *afʿaltu* are used interchangeably in transitivity." It is also said: "The more apparent view is that the verb was made transitive by a preposition, which was then deleted, and the verb was connected directly to its object."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 5:

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾. The wuhush (wild beasts) is the plural of wahsh, which is the animal of the land that by its nature is not sociable with the children of Adam. What is intended by it is that which includes the cattle absolutely.

﴿Are gathered﴾, i.e., they are brought together from every side. This is just before the first blast, when a fire emerges, and people and livestock flee from it until they are gathered together. It has also been said: they are made to die, from the saying of them: "When the year (drought) has starved the people, it has gathered them (ḥashara-hum)." Similar to this is what ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Mujahid that he said: "Their gathering (ḥashr) is their death." And from Ibn ʿAbbas, the interpretation of ḥashr as "gathering," except that he said, as a group narrated and al-Ḥakim authenticated: they are gathered by death, so they are not resurrected, and no one is brought to the Resurrection except the two species (jinn and humankind). It has also been said: they are resurrected for retaliation, so every creature is gathered, even the fly. This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Qatadah and a group. In a narration from the scholar (al-Ḥabr, i.e., Ibn ʿAbbas): the wild beasts are gathered until retaliation is exacted among them, one for another, so retaliation is exacted for the hornless sheep from the horned sheep; then it is said to them, "Be dust," and they become dust. It has also been said: when judgment is passed among them, they are returned to dust, so nothing remains of them except what brings joy to the children of Adam and admiration for its form, such as the peacock and the gazelle. It has also been said: everything that did not benefit a person remains, except the believer, like a sheep of which he ate none; and what remains will enter Paradise in a state fitting for it. Many scholars went to the resurrection of all animals, inclining to these reports and the like.

Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning this verse that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rights will surely be rendered to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, to the extent that the hornless sheep will be given retaliation from the horned sheep."

Ahmad ibn Hanbal added: "And even the ant from the ant."

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali and a group inclined to the view that none is gathered except the two species, since it is not morally responsible except one fit for honour in some respect; and there is no text from the Book or the Sunnah on which reliance is placed that indicates the gathering of other than them among the wild beasts. The report of Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, although authentic, did not come as an explanation of the verse, and it may be a metaphor for complete justice. To this view I incline, and I do not assert the error of those who hold the first view, because they have what can serve as a basis in general. And Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read ﴿ḥušširat﴾ with the doubled letter, for intensiveness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 6:

﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾ That is: they are heated, such that their waters recede and the fire appears in their place. Therefore it has been reported, regarding what is said, that "the sea is the covering of Jahannam" (jahannam). Or they are filled by causing some of them to burst into others, until their salty and sweet waters become one sea, from "sajara al-tannur" (he filled the oven) when he filled it with firewood in order to heat it. It is also said: they are filled with fires blazing to torment the people of the Fire. It is also said: they are filled with earth, leveling them with the ground of the Gathering (al-mahshar), but there is no established basis for this transmitted from the early generation (al-salaf). Al-Zarkashi (al-Bahr) reported from the book Lughat al-Qur'an that ﴿sujjirat﴾ means "gathered," in the dialect of Khath'am, and perhaps their gathering in this sense is by bursting. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that the meaning is: they are made to possess (mulikat), and their turbulence is restrained so that they do not overflow the earth out of terror, and this would be derived from "sajur al-kalb" (the dog's collar), which is a piece of wood placed around its neck; and it is said: "sajarahu" when he tied it with it. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited: «sujirat» with the lighter pronunciation.

﴿And when the souls are paired﴾. That is: each soul is joined with its like. A group of narrators, among them al-Hakim (al-Hakim al-Naysaburi), who also graded it sound, transmitted from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked about this and said: "A righteous man is joined with a righteous man in Paradise, and an evil man is joined with an evil man in the Fire. That is the pairing of souls." In a raised (marfu') hadith that al-Nu'man also narrated, its apparent meaning implies this. Some said: this refers to the place of standing (al-Mawqif, the station of standing before Allah on the Day of Judgment), that the ranks are joined together: the prophets, then the saints, then the most excellent after the most excellent. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the souls of the believers are joined with their spouses from the wide-eyed maidens (al-Hur) and others, and the souls of the disbelievers are joined with the devils. It was also said: each soul is joined with its record (kitab), and it was said: with its deeds. It was also permitted that the meaning is: each soul is joined with its adversary, so it cannot escape from him. You know that each soul having an adversary is a remote possibility. In any case, "nafs" here means the self (dhat), and "tazwij" means making a thing a pair (zawj), i.e., a companion. Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi said: the souls are joined with their spouses, and this occurs at the Resurrection (al-Ba'th); according to this view "nafs" means the spirit (ruh). Asim read «زُوِّجَتْ» in the form «فُوعِلَتْ» (fu'ilat), a variant reading of the verb.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 8–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when the girl buried alive is asked﴾ — and she is the daughter who is buried alive, from al-wa'd (wa'd, "heaviness"). She was named thus because she is weighed down with earth until she dies. It has been said: it is a metathesis of al-awtad (the tent-pegs). Al-Murtada related this in his Durar from some of the lexicographers, but Abu Hayyan did not accept it. The Arabs used to bury daughters alive out of fear of shame coming upon them because of them. It has also been said: out of fear of poverty; perhaps this applies to some of them. Among them were those who said: the angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is He above what they say, so they attributed daughters to Him, the Most High, and He, the Mighty and Majestic, is more worthy of them. Many have mentioned that when a man among them had a daughter born to him and wished to keep her alive, he would dress her in a woollen or hair garment, to tend the camels and sheep for him in the desert. If he wished to kill her, he would leave her until she reached six years of age. Then he would say to her mother: "Perfume her and adorn her, so that I may take her to her in-laws," and he would have dug a well for her in the desert. He would bring her to the well and say to her: "Look into it." Then he would push her from behind and pour earth over her until the well was levelled with the ground. It has also been said: when a pregnant woman drew near her time, she would dig a pit and give birth over the mouth of the pit. If she bore a girl, she threw her into it; if she bore a boy, she kept him. I read in some books, when I was a youth, that the first tribe among the Arabs to bury daughters was Rabi'a. That was because they raided a people and a daughter of their leader was seized; he later recovered her after a settlement, and she was given the choice, with his consent, between her father and the one with whom she was staying. She chose the one she was with and preferred him over her father. He became angry and instituted burying daughters as a rule, and they did so out of jealousy and fear that something like what had befallen them would happen to them again. It spread among the Arabs and others. And Allah knows best the soundness of this.

Al-Bazzi, in one transmission, read: "al-ma'udah" (like ma'unah). It is possible that the original is "al-mau'udah" as in the reading of the majority, and the vowel of the hamza was moved to the preceding waw, the waw was deleted, and then that waw was hamzated. It is also possible that it is an ism maf'ul from "ada," the original being "al-ma'udah," with one of the two waws deleted, so it became "al-mau'udah," as "maqul" became "maqul" by deletion. It was also read "al-mawudah," with a damma on the first waw and facilitation of the hamza, meaning facilitation by deleting it and moving its vowel to the letter before it. In Majma' al-Bayan (the responsibility for which lies with its author), it is related from Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Abd Allah, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that they read "al-mawaddah" with a fatha on the mim and the waw, meaning by it kinship and relationship. From Abu Ja'far: the kinship of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The killing of it may mean severing it, or it may be literal, with the attribution being metaphorical, and what is meant is the killing of the one characterised by it. The directing of the question to the buried girl in His saying, "when she is asked, for what sin was she killed," rather than to the one who buries her, although the sin belongs to him rather than to her, is for her consolation, to show complete anger and displeasure toward her burier, and to remove him from the rank of direct address, with intensified rebuke. For when the victim is questioned in the presence of the aggressor, and the crime is attributed to the victim rather than to the aggressor, this prompts the aggressor to reflect on his own state and the state of the victim, so that he sees the innocence of the victim and that he himself is the one deserving of reproach and punishment. This is a kind of gradual leading-on, occurring by way of allusion, as in His saying, "Did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, and Ibn Ya'mur read "su'ilat" (was asked), that is: she disputed, or she asked Allah, or she was asked by her killer. It was said, "qutilat" (was killed), because the speech is a report about her, not a quotation of what she was addressed with when asked, so as to say "qutilat" in the second person, nor a quotation of her words when she asked, so as to say "qutilat" as her own report about herself. 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud also, Jabir ibn Yazid, Abu al-Duha, and Mujahid read it likewise. al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "sīlat" with a kasra on the sin, according to the dialect of those who say "sala" without hamza. Abu Ja'far read it with a shadda on the ya', because "al-mau'udah" is a noun of genus, so the plural sense is appropriate, with regard to the individuals. In the verse there is evidence of the enormity of the crime of burying daughters.

Al-Bazzar and al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Qays ibn 'Asim al-Tamimi came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'I buried eight daughters of mine in the Jahiliyya.' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Free a slave for each one.' He said: 'I am a owner of camels.' He said: 'Then sacrifice a camel for each one.'"

This command is for recommendation, not obligation, because the soundness of repentance depends upon it, for Islam wipes out what came before it of such matters. In it is the magnification of the matter of burying. Among the Arabs were some who found it repugnant, such as Sa'sa'a ibn Najiya al-Mujashi'i, grandfather of al-Farazdaq, who used to ransom the buried girls from his people, the Banu Tamim, and al-Farazdaq boasted of this in his saying:

"My grandfather who prevented the burying women, and gave life to the buried, so she was not buried."

Al-Tabarani related from him that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I did deeds in the Jahiliyya; is there any reward for them? I gave life to three hundred and sixty of the buried girls, buying each one of them with two ten-month-old she-camels and a stallion. Is there any reward for me in that?' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'You have its reward, since Allah has bestowed Islam upon you.'"

Coitus interruptus (al-'azl) is counted as a kind of burying, for Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Khudhama bint Wahb, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about al-'azl, and he said: 'That is the hidden burying.'"

From here it has been said it is forbidden, and you know that the question is a matter of difference of opinion. Imam al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "al-'azl is that one copulates, and when he nears ejaculation he withdraws and ejaculates outside the vagina. It is disliked according to us in every case of a woman, whether she consents or not, because it is a means to cutting off offspring. As for prohibition, our companions — meaning the Shafi'is — said: it is not forbidden with a slave-woman he owns, nor with his free wife who is a slave, whether she consents or not, because there is harm to his slave-woman in her becoming an umm walad and the impossibility of selling her; and there is harm to his enslaved wife in her child becoming a slave following its mother. As for his free wife, if she gives permission it is not forbidden; otherwise there are two opinions, the more correct of which is that it is not forbidden. Then the hadiths whose apparent meaning conflict on this topic are reconciled by holding that those which contain prohibition are to be understood as reprehensible in the sense of disliked by way of caution, and those which contain permission are to be understood as meaning it is not unlawful, but its meaning is not negation of disliking." End of quotation.

It has been answered regarding the preceding hadith that calling it hidden burying does not indicate that its ruling is the ruling of open burying; for it is soundly established that ostentation is hidden shirk, and no one has said its ruling is the ruling of shirk. It is not far-fetched that masturbation is like coitus interruptus, a hidden burying. Some have mentioned that if one does not fear fornication, it is forbidden, and if one does fear it, it is not forbidden. Likewise, it is not far-fetched that intercourse between the thighs with one whom it is lawful for him to have intercourse with is similar; but I have not seen anyone who holds it forbidden. The full discussion of this matter is in the books of jurisprudence, so let them be consulted.

Al-Zamakhshari used the verse as evidence that the children of polytheists are not punished, and that punishment is not deserved except through sin. As for the first, the rebuke of her killer is incompatible with her punishment, because the deserving of rebuke is for her innocence from sin; so when He, glorified is He, rebukes the unbeliever with her innocence from sin, how would He then turn upon her and do to her what would cause the rebuked one to forget the everlasting punishment? As for the second, it is because of the indication of His saying, "for what sin was she killed," that killing is only resorted to for a sin, and that it is not deemed good to commit it without one; and it is known that in its meaning is every punishment. Then, since the verse shows that the buried girl had no sin, so that the rebuke might be complete, it implies that she does not deserve punishment. It has been claimed that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about this and argued with this verse, and it was objected that the basis of what he mentioned is the notion of good and evil, and what is in these two has been explained in its place. And even granting it, we do not concede that the cause of rebuke is restricted to innocence; for the killing was for the motive mentioned in the Qur'an, namely fear of poverty, which is a vice that deserves rebuke, and the one killed deserved the punishment of the Hereafter first. The indication of the verse is that their motive for killing was not a sin; it is not an indication that the sin — that is, what makes the buried girl deserve punishment — is absent in every respect. And what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, we do not accept its soundness, and there are reports that contradict it.

Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and others related from Salama ibn Yazid al-Ju'fi, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "The one who buries and the one buried are in the Fire, unless the one who buries reaches Islam, and Allah pardons her."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the children of polytheists, and he said: 'Allah, when He created them, knows best what they would have done.'"

Its interpretation, as has been said, is what Abu Dawud related from 'A'isha: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the offspring of believers?' He said: 'They are from their fathers.' I said: 'Without any deed?' He said: 'Allah knows best what they would have done.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, and the offspring of polytheists?' He said: 'They are from their fathers.' I said: 'Without any deed?' He said: 'Allah knows best what they would have done.'"

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad: "Khadija asked about two boys, what about them in the Jahiliyya? The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'They are in the Fire.'" And you know that in the matter of children, from this aspect, there is what is other than the children of prophets, peace be upon them, for they are agreed to be of the people of Paradise, as al-Laqqani said, unlike... Imam al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "All scholars of the Muslims whose opinion counts have agreed that whoever of the children of Muslims dies is among the people of Paradise, because he is not morally responsible. Some whose opinion does not count have hesitated concerning it, on the hadith of 'A'isha: 'A boy of the Ansar died, and she said: Blessed is he, a sparrow of the sparrows of Paradise, who did not do evil and did not reach it. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Or otherwise, O 'A'isha? Allah created for Paradise people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins, and He created for the Fire people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins."'"

The scholars answered this by saying: perhaps he, peace be upon him, forbade her from hastening to a definitive judgment without having a conclusive proof; and it is possible that he, peace be upon him, said this before he knew that the children of Muslims are in Paradise. When he knew, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in his saying: "No Muslim whose three children have died before reaching puberty, but Allah will admit him to Paradise by His grace and mercy toward them." And other hadiths. As for the children of polytheists, there are three opinions. The majority said: they are in the Fire, following their fathers, on the hadith: "He was asked about the children of polytheists who die young, and he, peace be upon him, said: Allah knows best what they would have done." That is: and other than that. A group withheld judgment concerning them. A third said — and this is the sound view held by the verifiers — that they are of the people of Paradise, and evidence for it is adduced

with things among them: "The hadith of Abraham the Friend (peace be upon him), when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in Paradise with the children of mankind around him. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, and the children of the polytheists?' He said: 'And the children of the polytheists.'" Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih.

Among them is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never punish until We had sent a messenger﴾. Moral accountability (taklif) does not apply to a newborn, and it is bound by the word of the Messenger until he reaches maturity (bulugh). This is agreed upon. As for the reply to the hadith: "Allah knows best what they were doing," it contains no explicit statement that they are in the Fire. The literal meaning of the expression "Allah knows best what they were doing" is: whether they reached maturity or not, and accountability applies only upon reaching maturity. End of quotation. The possibility he mentioned in the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, has been criticized on the grounds that it is contradicted by what he mentioned of the hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him). The hadith of Aisha took place in Medina, because it concerned a child of the Ansar, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) consummation of marriage with her took place there. The hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him) took place in Mecca, because the apparent view is that that vision was on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension), and he (ﷺ) was in Mecca at that time. From this it is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that all children were in Paradise on that day. How, then, can it be supposed that what he said afterward was said before he knew that the children of the Muslims were in Paradise? Also, if the hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him) was in Mecca, it weakens the first reply concerning the hadith of Aisha, by the possibility that she said what she said because that hadith had reached her. Then, what was mentioned, that the positions regarding the children of the polytheists are three, apparently is based on what has been reported to him; otherwise, they are not limited to these. Among them is that they are in a barzakh (intermediate state) between Paradise and the Fire. Among them is that they will be tested by entering the Fire on the Day of Resurrection: whoever has been destined for happiness will obey by entering it and will be returned to Paradise, and whoever has been destined for wretchedness will refuse and will be dragged into the Fire, as came in some narrations. So no specific one of them is judged to be in Paradise or in the Fire. On this basis, the saying "Allah knows best what they were doing" is interpreted. In the preferred opinions of Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, this is the best of the replies concerning them. Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti said: it is the correct and relied-upon view. Among them is what this Jalal mentioned and what Imam al-Rabbani al-Faruqi al-Sirhindi, may Allah sanctify his secret, chose: that they will be gathered and then become dust like wild beasts. If what was mentioned earlier, that they are in Paradise, is meant as their being there in the same way as the rest of its people, then there is another opinion, which is that they are there as servants to its people. Al-Nasafi transmitted this in Bahr al-Kalam ('Ala Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah), and in it there are many hadiths. The apparent view is that what is meant by the children of the polytheists is the children who were born to them while they were polytheists, even if they later believed. This is indicated by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The one who was predestined in the case of the two sons of Khadija: they are in the Fire."

This contradicts those who say: the children of those who died as polytheists are in the Fire, and the children of the polytheists who believed after their death are in Paradise as an honour to them. What I choose is the view that children, absolutely, as well as the child of fornication and one who became insane before puberty, are in Paradise. This is most fitting to the generosity of Allah, exalted is He, and His vast mercy, and most in accordance with wisdom according to the apparent meaning, and most supported by the verses. There is no improbability in preferring the reports that indicate this, with what has been mentioned, over the reports that indicate the opposite. As for the claim that what those reports contain came from him (peace be upon him) before he knew that children are in Paradise, it is far-fetched in my view. Yes, it is permissible that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that they are among the people of the Fire on the basis of revelation about this, like his reports of the threats from which Allah, exalted is He, pardons, since it is conditional upon a condition that did not include them, for example the grace; but it was not mentioned with it, just as it was not mentioned with them, for a wisdom. Then he (peace be upon him) informed that they are among the people of Paradise, also on the basis of revelation about this, and this would include the report that the condition for their being among the people of the Fire is not fulfilled, out of grace and generosity from Allah, exalted is He. That would be like pardoning what the threat requires. Similar to this is his report of what was mentioned, on the basis of witnessing their being in Paradise with Abraham (peace be upon him). So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 8–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when the girl buried alive is asked﴾ — and she is the daughter who is buried alive, from al-wa'd (wa'd, "heaviness"). She was named thus because she is weighed down with earth until she dies. It has been said: it is a metathesis of al-awtad (the tent-pegs). Al-Murtada related this in his Durar from some of the lexicographers, but Abu Hayyan did not accept it. The Arabs used to bury daughters alive out of fear of shame coming upon them because of them. It has also been said: out of fear of poverty; perhaps this applies to some of them. Among them were those who said: the angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is He above what they say, so they attributed daughters to Him, the Most High, and He, the Mighty and Majestic, is more worthy of them. Many have mentioned that when a man among them had a daughter born to him and wished to keep her alive, he would dress her in a woollen or hair garment, to tend the camels and sheep for him in the desert. If he wished to kill her, he would leave her until she reached six years of age. Then he would say to her mother: "Perfume her and adorn her, so that I may take her to her in-laws," and he would have dug a well for her in the desert. He would bring her to the well and say to her: "Look into it." Then he would push her from behind and pour earth over her until the well was levelled with the ground. It has also been said: when a pregnant woman drew near her time, she would dig a pit and give birth over the mouth of the pit. If she bore a girl, she threw her into it; if she bore a boy, she kept him. I read in some books, when I was a youth, that the first tribe among the Arabs to bury daughters was Rabi'a. That was because they raided a people and a daughter of their leader was seized; he later recovered her after a settlement, and she was given the choice, with his consent, between her father and the one with whom she was staying. She chose the one she was with and preferred him over her father. He became angry and instituted burying daughters as a rule, and they did so out of jealousy and fear that something like what had befallen them would happen to them again. It spread among the Arabs and others. And Allah knows best the soundness of this.

Al-Bazzi, in one transmission, read: "al-ma'udah" (like ma'unah). It is possible that the original is "al-mau'udah" as in the reading of the majority, and the vowel of the hamza was moved to the preceding waw, the waw was deleted, and then that waw was hamzated. It is also possible that it is an ism maf'ul from "ada," the original being "al-ma'udah," with one of the two waws deleted, so it became "al-mau'udah," as "maqul" became "maqul" by deletion. It was also read "al-mawudah," with a damma on the first waw and facilitation of the hamza, meaning facilitation by deleting it and moving its vowel to the letter before it. In Majma' al-Bayan (the responsibility for which lies with its author), it is related from Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Abd Allah, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that they read "al-mawaddah" with a fatha on the mim and the waw, meaning by it kinship and relationship. From Abu Ja'far: the kinship of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The killing of it may mean severing it, or it may be literal, with the attribution being metaphorical, and what is meant is the killing of the one characterised by it. The directing of the question to the buried girl in His saying, "when she is asked, for what sin was she killed," rather than to the one who buries her, although the sin belongs to him rather than to her, is for her consolation, to show complete anger and displeasure toward her burier, and to remove him from the rank of direct address, with intensified rebuke. For when the victim is questioned in the presence of the aggressor, and the crime is attributed to the victim rather than to the aggressor, this prompts the aggressor to reflect on his own state and the state of the victim, so that he sees the innocence of the victim and that he himself is the one deserving of reproach and punishment. This is a kind of gradual leading-on, occurring by way of allusion, as in His saying, "Did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, and Ibn Ya'mur read "su'ilat" (was asked), that is: she disputed, or she asked Allah, or she was asked by her killer. It was said, "qutilat" (was killed), because the speech is a report about her, not a quotation of what she was addressed with when asked, so as to say "qutilat" in the second person, nor a quotation of her words when she asked, so as to say "qutilat" as her own report about herself. 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud also, Jabir ibn Yazid, Abu al-Duha, and Mujahid read it likewise. al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "sīlat" with a kasra on the sin, according to the dialect of those who say "sala" without hamza. Abu Ja'far read it with a shadda on the ya', because "al-mau'udah" is a noun of genus, so the plural sense is appropriate, with regard to the individuals. In the verse there is evidence of the enormity of the crime of burying daughters.

Al-Bazzar and al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Qays ibn 'Asim al-Tamimi came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'I buried eight daughters of mine in the Jahiliyya.' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Free a slave for each one.' He said: 'I am a owner of camels.' He said: 'Then sacrifice a camel for each one.'"

This command is for recommendation, not obligation, because the soundness of repentance depends upon it, for Islam wipes out what came before it of such matters. In it is the magnification of the matter of burying. Among the Arabs were some who found it repugnant, such as Sa'sa'a ibn Najiya al-Mujashi'i, grandfather of al-Farazdaq, who used to ransom the buried girls from his people, the Banu Tamim, and al-Farazdaq boasted of this in his saying:

"My grandfather who prevented the burying women, and gave life to the buried, so she was not buried."

Al-Tabarani related from him that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I did deeds in the Jahiliyya; is there any reward for them? I gave life to three hundred and sixty of the buried girls, buying each one of them with two ten-month-old she-camels and a stallion. Is there any reward for me in that?' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'You have its reward, since Allah has bestowed Islam upon you.'"

Coitus interruptus (al-'azl) is counted as a kind of burying, for Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Khudhama bint Wahb, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about al-'azl, and he said: 'That is the hidden burying.'"

From here it has been said it is forbidden, and you know that the question is a matter of difference of opinion. Imam al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "al-'azl is that one copulates, and when he nears ejaculation he withdraws and ejaculates outside the vagina. It is disliked according to us in every case of a woman, whether she consents or not, because it is a means to cutting off offspring. As for prohibition, our companions — meaning the Shafi'is — said: it is not forbidden with a slave-woman he owns, nor with his free wife who is a slave, whether she consents or not, because there is harm to his slave-woman in her becoming an umm walad and the impossibility of selling her; and there is harm to his enslaved wife in her child becoming a slave following its mother. As for his free wife, if she gives permission it is not forbidden; otherwise there are two opinions, the more correct of which is that it is not forbidden. Then the hadiths whose apparent meaning conflict on this topic are reconciled by holding that those which contain prohibition are to be understood as reprehensible in the sense of disliked by way of caution, and those which contain permission are to be understood as meaning it is not unlawful, but its meaning is not negation of disliking." End of quotation.

It has been answered regarding the preceding hadith that calling it hidden burying does not indicate that its ruling is the ruling of open burying; for it is soundly established that ostentation is hidden shirk, and no one has said its ruling is the ruling of shirk. It is not far-fetched that masturbation is like coitus interruptus, a hidden burying. Some have mentioned that if one does not fear fornication, it is forbidden, and if one does fear it, it is not forbidden. Likewise, it is not far-fetched that intercourse between the thighs with one whom it is lawful for him to have intercourse with is similar; but I have not seen anyone who holds it forbidden. The full discussion of this matter is in the books of jurisprudence, so let them be consulted.

Al-Zamakhshari used the verse as evidence that the children of polytheists are not punished, and that punishment is not deserved except through sin. As for the first, the rebuke of her killer is incompatible with her punishment, because the deserving of rebuke is for her innocence from sin; so when He, glorified is He, rebukes the unbeliever with her innocence from sin, how would He then turn upon her and do to her what would cause the rebuked one to forget the everlasting punishment? As for the second, it is because of the indication of His saying, "for what sin was she killed," that killing is only resorted to for a sin, and that it is not deemed good to commit it without one; and it is known that in its meaning is every punishment. Then, since the verse shows that the buried girl had no sin, so that the rebuke might be complete, it implies that she does not deserve punishment. It has been claimed that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about this and argued with this verse, and it was objected that the basis of what he mentioned is the notion of good and evil, and what is in these two has been explained in its place. And even granting it, we do not concede that the cause of rebuke is restricted to innocence; for the killing was for the motive mentioned in the Qur'an, namely fear of poverty, which is a vice that deserves rebuke, and the one killed deserved the punishment of the Hereafter first. The indication of the verse is that their motive for killing was not a sin; it is not an indication that the sin — that is, what makes the buried girl deserve punishment — is absent in every respect. And what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, we do not accept its soundness, and there are reports that contradict it.

Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and others related from Salama ibn Yazid al-Ju'fi, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "The one who buries and the one buried are in the Fire, unless the one who buries reaches Islam, and Allah pardons her."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the children of polytheists, and he said: 'Allah, when He created them, knows best what they would have done.'"

Its interpretation, as has been said, is what Abu Dawud related from 'A'isha: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the offspring of believers?' He said: 'They are from their fathers.' I said: 'Without any deed?' He said: 'Allah knows best what they would have done.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, and the offspring of polytheists?' He said: 'They are from their fathers.' I said: 'Without any deed?' He said: 'Allah knows best what they would have done.'"

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad: "Khadija asked about two boys, what about them in the Jahiliyya? The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'They are in the Fire.'" And you know that in the matter of children, from this aspect, there is what is other than the children of prophets, peace be upon them, for they are agreed to be of the people of Paradise, as al-Laqqani said, unlike... Imam al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "All scholars of the Muslims whose opinion counts have agreed that whoever of the children of Muslims dies is among the people of Paradise, because he is not morally responsible. Some whose opinion does not count have hesitated concerning it, on the hadith of 'A'isha: 'A boy of the Ansar died, and she said: Blessed is he, a sparrow of the sparrows of Paradise, who did not do evil and did not reach it. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Or otherwise, O 'A'isha? Allah created for Paradise people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins, and He created for the Fire people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins."'"

The scholars answered this by saying: perhaps he, peace be upon him, forbade her from hastening to a definitive judgment without having a conclusive proof; and it is possible that he, peace be upon him, said this before he knew that the children of Muslims are in Paradise. When he knew, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in his saying: "No Muslim whose three children have died before reaching puberty, but Allah will admit him to Paradise by His grace and mercy toward them." And other hadiths. As for the children of polytheists, there are three opinions. The majority said: they are in the Fire, following their fathers, on the hadith: "He was asked about the children of polytheists who die young, and he, peace be upon him, said: Allah knows best what they would have done." That is: and other than that. A group withheld judgment concerning them. A third said — and this is the sound view held by the verifiers — that they are of the people of Paradise, and evidence for it is adduced

with things among them: "The hadith of Abraham the Friend (peace be upon him), when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in Paradise with the children of mankind around him. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, and the children of the polytheists?' He said: 'And the children of the polytheists.'" Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih.

Among them is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never punish until We had sent a messenger﴾. Moral accountability (taklif) does not apply to a newborn, and it is bound by the word of the Messenger until he reaches maturity (bulugh). This is agreed upon. As for the reply to the hadith: "Allah knows best what they were doing," it contains no explicit statement that they are in the Fire. The literal meaning of the expression "Allah knows best what they were doing" is: whether they reached maturity or not, and accountability applies only upon reaching maturity. End of quotation. The possibility he mentioned in the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, has been criticized on the grounds that it is contradicted by what he mentioned of the hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him). The hadith of Aisha took place in Medina, because it concerned a child of the Ansar, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) consummation of marriage with her took place there. The hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him) took place in Mecca, because the apparent view is that that vision was on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension), and he (ﷺ) was in Mecca at that time. From this it is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that all children were in Paradise on that day. How, then, can it be supposed that what he said afterward was said before he knew that the children of the Muslims were in Paradise? Also, if the hadith of Abraham (peace be upon him) was in Mecca, it weakens the first reply concerning the hadith of Aisha, by the possibility that she said what she said because that hadith had reached her. Then, what was mentioned, that the positions regarding the children of the polytheists are three, apparently is based on what has been reported to him; otherwise, they are not limited to these. Among them is that they are in a barzakh (intermediate state) between Paradise and the Fire. Among them is that they will be tested by entering the Fire on the Day of Resurrection: whoever has been destined for happiness will obey by entering it and will be returned to Paradise, and whoever has been destined for wretchedness will refuse and will be dragged into the Fire, as came in some narrations. So no specific one of them is judged to be in Paradise or in the Fire. On this basis, the saying "Allah knows best what they were doing" is interpreted. In the preferred opinions of Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, this is the best of the replies concerning them. Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti said: it is the correct and relied-upon view. Among them is what this Jalal mentioned and what Imam al-Rabbani al-Faruqi al-Sirhindi, may Allah sanctify his secret, chose: that they will be gathered and then become dust like wild beasts. If what was mentioned earlier, that they are in Paradise, is meant as their being there in the same way as the rest of its people, then there is another opinion, which is that they are there as servants to its people. Al-Nasafi transmitted this in Bahr al-Kalam ('Ala Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah), and in it there are many hadiths. The apparent view is that what is meant by the children of the polytheists is the children who were born to them while they were polytheists, even if they later believed. This is indicated by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The one who was predestined in the case of the two sons of Khadija: they are in the Fire."

This contradicts those who say: the children of those who died as polytheists are in the Fire, and the children of the polytheists who believed after their death are in Paradise as an honour to them. What I choose is the view that children, absolutely, as well as the child of fornication and one who became insane before puberty, are in Paradise. This is most fitting to the generosity of Allah, exalted is He, and His vast mercy, and most in accordance with wisdom according to the apparent meaning, and most supported by the verses. There is no improbability in preferring the reports that indicate this, with what has been mentioned, over the reports that indicate the opposite. As for the claim that what those reports contain came from him (peace be upon him) before he knew that children are in Paradise, it is far-fetched in my view. Yes, it is permissible that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that they are among the people of the Fire on the basis of revelation about this, like his reports of the threats from which Allah, exalted is He, pardons, since it is conditional upon a condition that did not include them, for example the grace; but it was not mentioned with it, just as it was not mentioned with them, for a wisdom. Then he (peace be upon him) informed that they are among the people of Paradise, also on the basis of revelation about this, and this would include the report that the condition for their being among the people of the Fire is not fulfilled, out of grace and generosity from Allah, exalted is He. That would be like pardoning what the threat requires. Similar to this is his report of what was mentioned, on the basis of witnessing their being in Paradise with Abraham (peace be upon him). So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 10:

﴿And when the pages are spread open﴾. That is, the pages of deeds (ṣuḥuf al-a'māl). Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "When a person dies, his page is folded up, and then it is spread open on the Day of Resurrection, and he is called to account for what is in it." It was also said: "nushirat" means: they were distributed among their owners. From Murthid ibn Wada'a: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the pages will fly out from beneath the Throne. The page of the believer will fall into his hand in a lofty garden, and the page of the disbeliever will fall into his hand amid scorching wind and boiling water." That is, what is written in them is that; and these are pages other than the pages of deeds.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "nushshirat" with the doubled letter (shadda), for emphasis in the spreading, in both of its meanings, or because of the great number of pages, or because of the intensity of the flying about.

Qur'an 81:11: ﴿And when the sky is stripped away﴾ — it is torn off and removed, just as the hide is stripped from a slaughtered animal, and as a covering is uncovered from the thing it conceals. The root of kashṭ (stripping, flaying) is skinning, and it is used here metaphorically for removal. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿qushitat﴾ with a qaf in place of the kaf, and the interchange of the two letters is not rare, as in al-kafur and al-qafur. It is pure Arabic, quhhun and kuhhun (i.e., both forms are authentic Arabic).

And when the Blazing Fire is kindled (wa-idha al-jahimu su'-‘irat). That is: it was set ablaze with a fierce kindling. Qatadah said: "Its kindling was caused by the wrath of Allah the Exalted and the sins of the children of Adam." And a group of reciters, among them ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face), read «su'irat» with the light (takhfif) form.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 13:

﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾: i.e., it is brought near to the God-fearing, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far away﴾. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah that he said: "Six verses of this surah are in this world while people are looking on, and six are in the Hereafter: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ – to – ﴿and when the seas are set boiling﴾, these are in this world; ﴿and when the souls are paired﴾ – to – ﴿and when Paradise is brought near﴾, this is in the Hereafter."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "Six signs come before the Day of Resurrection: while people are in their markets, the light of the sun goes away. While they are in that state, the stars become dim. While they are in that state, the mountains fall upon the face of the earth, and they shake and tremble. The jinn flee to mankind and mankind to the jinn, and the beasts, birds and wild animals become mixed together, and they surge against one another. The pregnant she-camels are left neglected. The jinn say to mankind: 'We will bring you the news,' so they set off to the sea and find it is a blazing fire. While they are in that state, the earth splits open with a single crack. While they are in that state, a wind comes upon them and causes them to die."

Some scholars said: the first six are between the two blasts of the Trumpet, and this is the intended meaning of those who said they are in this world. It was also said: they are before the first blast and what follows it up to the second blast. So do not be heedless.

﴿عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ ما أحْضَرَتْ﴾ [A soul will know what it has presented.] This is the response (jawab) to ﴿إذا﴾ [when], on the basis that the time meant here is a single extended period. It includes the matters mentioned, and it begins shortly before the First Blast, or with it, and ends with the decisive judgment among creation. However, this does not mean that the soul knows what it knows throughout every part of that long period, nor at the occurrence of each one of those calamities. Rather, it knows at the spreading of the scrolls. Yet, since some of those calamities are among its beginnings and some among its consequences, their knowledge is attributed to the time when all of them occur, to magnify the matter and to make the situation appear dreadful.

By ﴿ما أحْضَرَتْ﴾ [what it has presented] is meant its deeds, good and bad. As for the presenting of deeds, it may be the presenting of their scrolls, as the spreading of the scrolls indicates, or it may be the presenting of the deeds themselves, according to those who say that outward deeds in this life take on accidental forms, which appear in the Hereafter in substantial forms suited to them in goodness and ugliness, in specific modes and determined states, so that sins and disobedience take on bodies and become visible there. On this basis is interpreted the like of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ أمْوالَ اليَتامى ظُلْمًا إنَّما يَأْكُلُونَ في بُطُونِهِمْ نارًا﴾ [Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies]. Something from Ibn 'Abbas supports this, and so does the hadith about the slaughtering of Death and similar reports. It has been said: there is no improbability in this, for do you not see that knowledge appears in the world of image-archetypes ('alam al-mithal) in the form of milk, as is not hidden from one who has experience of the conditions of the al-Hadarat al-Khamsa (the Five Presences)? It has been related from some of the great scholars that they witness their deeds in this life when they are raised up to heaven, and that this occurs in a kind of embodiment.

Whatever the case, attributing the presenting of deeds to the soul, although they are presented by the command of God, exalted is He, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَوْمَ تَجِدُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما عَمِلَتْ مِن خَيْرٍ مُحْضَرًا﴾ [the Day every soul will find what it has done of good presented], and so on, is because when it performed them in this world, it is as if it had presented them at the place of standing (al-mawqif). The meaning of its knowing them, according to the first interpretation, is its being apprised of them in detail in the scrolls, such that nothing of them escapes it, as is indicated by their saying: ﴿مالِ هَذا الكِتابِ لا يُغادِرُ صَغِيرَةً ولا كَبِيرَةً إلا أحْصاها﴾ [What is with this Book that it leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it]. According to the second interpretation, it witnesses them as they truly are. If they were good, it witnesses them in forms more beautiful than those it perceived in the world, because acts of obedience are never free of some kind of hardship. If they were evil, it witnesses them contrary to what they appeared to be in the world, for they had adorned them for it and agreed with its desires.

The indefiniteness of "soul" (nafs), which indicates that knowledge is established for a single soul or for some souls, is meant to signal that its being established for all of its individuals together is so manifest and clear that no shadow of doubt can approach it, a certainty known to everyone. Had it been expressed with a phrase indicating otherwise... And it is also a symbolic allusion that those souls who know what is mentioned, despite their abundance and the multiplicity of their numbers, are insignificant in relation to the majesty of the Lord of Glory, to whom are pointed some wonders of His affairs that indicate the greatness of His dominion, exalted is He.

In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari) it is stated that this is one of the reversed forms of their speech, in which they intend exaggeration in what is reversed from it. Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿رُبَما يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْ كانُوا مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims], whose meaning is "how many" but more emphatic. Also the saying of the poet:

"I may leave the opponent with fingers turned yellow,
as if his garments were stained with mulberry juice."

And you say to one of the commanders of the armies: "How many horsemen do you have?" and he says: "A horseman, perhaps, is with me," or "You will not lack a horseman with me," while he has troops (maqanib) of them. His purpose by that is to go to excess in multiplying his horsemen, but he intended to show his freedom from exaggeration, and that he is one who minimizes what he has, let alone inflating it. So he uses the language of minimization, and from it is understood the meaning of abundance accurately and with certainty. Al-Kashshaf explains that it conveys this meaning together with a particular benefit in each specific situation. It mentions that among the benefits here is the magnifying of the Day by the minimizing of the knowing souls, even though they are all of them, and the showing that this is a speech of utmost greatness and majesty, and that He who changes and transforms these great bodies into attributes and essences, the human souls are insignificant beside His power, glory be to Him, to the utmost degree of insignificance.

Abu al-Su'ud has critiqued this with remarks that are not free of scrutiny, as is not hidden from one of keen insight, let alone one of subtle judgment. It has also been permitted that this is to indicate that if any soul at that time knows what it has presented, it becomes obligatory upon every soul to correct its deeds, lest it be that soul which did what it presented. How much more so when every soul knows it, in the manner of your saying to one whom you advise: "Perhaps you will regret what you have done," and a person often regrets what he has done. You do not intend by this that his regret is hoped for, not certain, or rarely occurring. Rather, you intend that the sensible person must avoid a matter from which regret is expected or which rarely happens to him. How much more so when it is certain to occur and very frequent!

It is well known that the indefinite noun (nakira) here carries the meaning of generality, and it may be general in affirmative statements when the context or something similar requires that. Among this is the saying of Ibn 'Umar to one of the people of al-Sham who asked him about a muhrim who killed a locust, whether he should give a date as expiation for it: "A date is better than a locust."

It has been said: because of this generality, the beginning of the sentence with an indefinite noun was permitted. As for the saying of some who claim that there is no generality in it, and that the generality comes from the equal relation of the part to the individuals of the category, it has been said: this is based on the assumption that generality contradicts unity and singularity. And you know that this contradicts only comprehensive generality (shumuli), not distributive generality (badali). Some have said: it is not far-fetched to say that generality is gained by placing it in the sphere of negation in meaning, because ﴿عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ﴾ [a soul knows] means "no soul is ignorant," since affirming a thing necessarily entails negating its opposite. This is nothing, for otherwise every indefinite noun in affirmation would be general by this kind of interpretation.

It is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that a reciter recited this surah in his presence, and when he reached ﴿عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ ما أحْضَرَتْ﴾, he said: "Woe, the breaking of his back!"

[p. 57]

﴿فَلا أُقْسِمُ بِالخُنَّسِ﴾ *al-khunnas* is the plural of *khānis*, from *al-khunūs*, which means *al-inqibāḍ* (drawing back, contracting) and *al-istikhfā'* (concealing oneself). ﴿الجَوارِ﴾ is the plural of *jāriya*, from *al-jary*, which means *al-marr al-sarī'* (swift passing). Its origin is the flowing of water and of whatever moves with its flow. ﴿الكُنَّسِ﴾ is the plural of *kānis* and *kānisa*, from *kanasa al-waḥsh*, meaning that the wild animal entered its *kinās*, which is its den that it makes from tree branches. According to what al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated, and which al-Hakim authenticated through a chain going back to Ali, may God ennoble his face, the intended meaning is the stars, meaning all of them. It was said that they are called *khunnas* because they recede during the day and are hidden from the eyes, and *kunnas* because they rise at night in their places, like the wild animals in their dens. The explanation of *takunisu* as *tatlu'* (rise) contains some obscurity. It was also said that they are called *khunnas* because they recede by day and are hidden from the eyes even while they are above the horizon, and they are *kunnas* because after rising they set and enter it, as gazelles enter the *kunus*, so that they are below the horizon after having been above it. The explanation of them as stars was also narrated from al-Hasan and Qatada.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "They are five planets: Saturn, Mercury, Jupiter, Bahram (meaning Mars), and Venus, and the *khunnas* are the retrograde ones, from *khanasa*, meaning he drew back."

They are described by what is mentioned in the verse because they move along with the sun and the moon, and they retrograde until they are hidden under the light of the sun. So their *khunūs* is their retrogression as seen from the earth, and their *kunūs* is their concealment under its light. They are called *al-mutaḥayyira* (the wandering ones) because of the variation of their states in their motion, as observed. They have direct motion, retrograde motion and stationary phases. Sometimes you see them moving in one direction, and then they are retrograde, moving in the opposite direction, and sometimes you see them moving and then they are stationary, not moving. The cause of this, according to what the earlier *ahl al-hay'a* (astronomers of the celestial configuration) said, is that they are on epicycles (*tadāwīr*) within deferents (*ḥawāmil*) of differing motions, as explained in its proper place. The later astronomers who deny what has been mentioned have other explanations, which are mentioned in their books. Together with the sun and the moon they are called *al-sayyārāt al-sab'* (the seven wandering stars), because their movement by their particular motion is something that is hardly hidden from anyone, unlike the other fixed stars (*al-thawābit*).

Al-Khatib, in his *Kitāb al-Nujūm*, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that these are the ones intended here. Describing them as *al-khunnas* in the sense of *al-rawājiʻ* (the retrograde ones) has been said to be an instance of *al-taghlīb* (the predominance of one term over another), since neither the sun nor the moon retrogrades. It was also said that they are called *khunnas* because they are hidden when they set. It was said: the two descriptions are considered in terms of their being hidden from the eyes and rising in their places in the manner previously mentioned, on the assumption that the intended meaning is all the stars.

That the wandering stars are these seven is what is known among the earlier astrologers. As for today, they have added other stars to them, called Vesta, Zuno, Pallas, Ceres, Uranus, and Hershel, which is the name of the astronomer who discovered it through observation. They have clarified their diameters, distances and motions. Were it not for fear of prolixity, I would have mentioned these details.

They also counted the earth among the wandering stars, based on their claim that it has a motion around the sun. It is well known that they did not count the moon among them, because according to them it is a satellite of the earth.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and a group of narrators, through several chains, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that they are the wild cattle. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas, and Abd ibn Humayd from Mujahid, Abu Maysara and al-Hasan, and al-Bahr (*Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*) reported it from al-Nakha'i, Jabir ibn Zayd and a group of others. Ibn Jarir narrated from the scholar Ibn Abbas (*al-Ḥabr*) that they are the gazelles, and this was also narrated from Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. They said: *al-khanas* is the receding of the nose behind the upper lip together with a slight elevation of the nose tip, and it is used to describe wild cattle and gazelles. From this is the saying of one of the later poets:

Not even the gazelle escapes, for all its beauty, from flaw,
nor the moon that is described [as flawless].

So the gazelle has a clear *khans*,
and the moon has a known *kalaf* (dark spots).
