﴿By the night when it turns away (or: when it approaches)﴾. That is, its darkness departs or arrives, and both interpretations are transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and others. According to al-Mubarrad, the word is among the *addad* (words that carry two opposite meanings). Al-Raghib said: *al-'as'asa* and *al-'sas* mean the thinning of darkness, which occurs at both ends of the night. Thus, in his view, it is a *mushtarak ma'nawi* (a term with a shared meaning, a single underlying sense) and not one of the *addad*. He interpreted ﴿'as'asa﴾ here as both "approached" and "withdrew" together, saying this applies to the beginning and the end of the night. Al-Farra' said: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of ﴿'as'asa﴾ is "withdrew" (adbara), and al-'Ajjaj, describing wine or the desert, supports this:

*Until, when the dawn breathed for it, and its night was lifted away from it and 'as'asa.*

It was also said that this is specifically the dialect of the Quraysh. It was further said that the meaning "its darkness approached" is more fitting with the words of the Most High, ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾, since it is the beginning of the day and so corresponds to the beginning of the night. It was said that the meaning "withdrew" is more suitable for this context, because of the close adjacency between the withdrawal of the night and the breathing of the dawn, so the relationship between them is one of proximity. What is meant by the dawn's breathing, as many have mentioned, is its illumination and its brightening. In al-Kashshaf: when the dawn approaches, a breeze and fresh air approach with its approach, and this is made into a "breath" for it by way of metaphor (majaz). It was also said: the dawn breathed, and by metaphor is meant an istiʿara (metaphor): since breath is a special wind that relieves the heart through expansion and contraction, that breeze was likened to breath, and the name was applied to it by istiʿara. The dawn was described as "breathing" because it accompanies it. So in the sentence there is an explicit metaphor (istiʿara muṣarraḥa) and a figurative use in the attribution (tajawwuz fi al-isnad).

The apparent meaning of some people's words is that, after the metaphor, this becomes a kinaya (metonymy) for illumination. It was also permitted that there is here a *makniyya* and a *takhyiliyya* (an implicit metaphor and an imaginative representation), by likening the dawn to a walker or one arriving from a great distance, and attributing to it breathing, meaning the blowing of its breeze, as a figurative imagining, as in ﴿they break the covenant of God﴾. Al-Imam said: the day, when the dark night overtakes it, is like one in distress, and just as he finds relief by breathing, so too the dawn is freed from darkness and its rising is as though it has escaped from distress into ease. This is more subtle than what al-Kashshaf intended, as is not hidden.

It was also permitted to say: when the night covered the day and pushed it beneath the earth, it was as though it had caused it to die and buried it. So the appearance of its light was likened to breathing, which indicates life. This is similar to what was reported from al-Imam. It was said: *tanaffasa* means it expanded and extended until it became day. The apparent meaning is that the breathing in the verse is an allusion to the true dawn (al-fajr al-thani al-sadiq), which is the one whose light spreads across the horizon in a transverse band, unlike the first, false dawn (al-fajr al-awwal al-kadhib), which appears elongated, its top brighter than the rest, and then vanishes and is followed by darkness, or diminishes until it is submerged in the second, according to the claim of some astronomers. Or its state varies in this, sometimes and sometimes, according to times and places, as has been said. This false dawn is called *'arid* (the glow). In the report of Muslim: "Let not the adhan of Bilal deceive you, nor this glow of the dawn-column until it spreads."

That is: until that generality spreads across the regions of the horizon. The words of some of the eminent scholars suggest that the verse contains an allusion to the false dawn, when he said: It is understood from calling the first dawn "'arid" in relation to the second that the light arising from it encounters a restraint shortly before the second dawn appears, as the breathing in the words of the Most High ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾ suggests. At that restraint something breathes out from it, like a kind of opening. What is observed in something restrained when part of it comes out at once is that its beginning is greater than its end, and from this is known the reason for the length of the column and the illumination of its top, to the end of what he said. There is a point of discussion in this.

Then, the apparent meaning is that the breathing of the dawn and its light occur through the sun's proximity to the eastern horizon by a fixed amount, which in the well-known view is eighteen degrees. As for al-Imam's claim that, on the basis of the earth's sphericity and the constant illumination of more than half of it by the sun, it follows that the appearance of light and the breathing of the dawn would occur whenever the sun departs from the meridian above the feet, and that this is shortly after midnight, the reality is contrary to this. It is a doubt about what is almost self-evident, and it involves neglect of the conditions of the earth's shadow and the reflection of rays from the eyes of the inhabitants of its regions. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

The waw in His words, exalted is He, ﴿By the dawn﴾ and ﴿by the night﴾, is, according to what is reported from Ibn Jinni, for conjunction (ʿatf).

(wa-idha) is not an object (maʿmul) of the verb of swearing, because that would corrupt the meaning, since restricting the oath by time is not intended, whether it is taken as a present (ḥal) or future (istiqbal) time. Rather, as many scholars have chosen, it is the object of an omitted noun (muḍaf muqaddar) such as "greatness" (ʿaẓama), because swearing by a thing is an exaltation of it. It is as if it were said: "And I do not swear by the greatness of the night at the time it grows dark (ʿasʿasa), nor by the greatness of the day at the time it breathes (tanaffasa)," in the manner of their saying: "How wonderful the lion when it pounces (idha sata)." For the meaning is not that the wonder is restricted to his awe and greatness at that time.

ʿIṣam al-Din said: It should be taken as a restriction of the thing sworn by, meaning: "I swear by the night being in the state of growing dark," and the ḥal is implied, meaning: its existence being determined at that time.

Al-ʿAllama al-Taftazani, in al-Talwih, explicitly stated concerning a similar case that (idha) is a badal (substitute) for "the night," since the intent is not to attach the oath to that time and restrict it by it. For this reason the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) prevented it from being a ḥal of "the night," because that too would restrict the oath to that time. Its relevance to this matter will come, God willing, in the commentary on Surat al-Shams, as well.

﴿Indeed it﴾, that is, the glorious Qur'an, which speaks of the terrifying calamities mentioned above. Taking the pronoun as referring to the report of the Resurrection and the Gathering is a forced interpretation (ta'assuf).

﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾. As Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and the majority (al-Jumhur) said, this is Jibril, peace be upon him. It is attributed to him, peace be upon him, because he is the intermediary in it and the one who conveys it from its sender, who is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Noble﴾ means honoured by Allah, glorified be He and exalted. It was also said: ﴿noble﴾ means compassionate towards the believers.

﴿Possessor of power﴾, that is, mighty, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Mighty in power﴾ (Q 53:5). It is reported concerning his power that he, peace be upon him, was sent to the cities of Lut, which were four cities, and in each city there were four hundred thousand fighting men, apart from the dhurriyy (offspring, non-combatants). He lifted them with those in them from the lowest earth until the people of the heavens heard the cries of the roosters and the barking of the dogs, then he overturned them and destroyed them.

It was also said: the intended meaning is power in performing the obedience of Allah, Exalted, and in not falling short of it, from the beginning of creation until the end of the time of taklif (legal accountability). It was also said: it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning is strength of memory and remoteness from forgetfulness and confusion.

﴿Near the Lord of the Throne, held in high regard﴾. That is: possessing an elevated status and nobility with God, the Mighty, may His majesty be exalted, a nearness of honour and distinction, not a nearness of place. So the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to "makin" (held in high regard), which is an intensive form (fa'il) from al-makana (status). Its use has become so common, as in al-Sihah (Mukhtar al-Sihah, the lexicon of al-Jawhari), that it was thought the letter mim belongs to the root of the word, and "tamakkana" (to become established) was derived from it, just as "tamaskana" (to feign poverty) was derived from al-maskana (poverty). It is also permitted that it be a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi) from al-kawn (being), its original form being "makwun" with the vowel of the waw being kasra; through transposition and conversion it became "makin," and by al-kawn is meant existence, as though, owing to the perfection of existence, it became the very essence of existence. The first is the apparent meaning. It has also been said that the adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element that stands as another attribute of "rasul" (messenger); that is: existing near the Lord of the Throne with the fitting existence. And that, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿Muṭāʿin﴾ (obeyed) among the nearest angels, peace be upon them, who issue forth from His command and return to His judgment.

﴿Thumma﴾ (then/there) is an adverb of place denoting distance. It may be an adverb governed by what precedes it, and it is taken as a reference to ﴿ʿinda dhī al-ʿarsh﴾ (with the Lord of the Throne). The meaning of his being obeyed there is that he is obeyed among the angels of God, the Most High, who are brought near, as you have heard. It may also be an adverb governed by what follows it, namely the Exalted One's words ﴿Amīnin﴾ (trustworthy), with the reference remaining as it is, and his trustworthiness concerns the revelation.

In a narration from him, peace be upon him, he said: "My trustworthiness is that I am not commanded with anything and then I exceed it to something else."

Part of his trustworthiness is that, peace be upon him, he enters the veils (ḥujub) without permission, as in some reports. Abū Jaʿfar, Abū Ḥaywa, Abū al-Barhasam and Ibn Miqsam recited ﴿thumma﴾ with a ḍamma on the thāʾ as a conjunction (ḥarf ʿatf), to magnify the trustworthiness and to clarify that it is the most excellent of his enumerated attributes. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ (Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ) said: it has the meaning of the waw (and), because Jibrīl, peace be upon him, possessed both attributes together at a single time. Had someone held that this conjunction carries the sense of sequence and delay, meaning "obeyed among the exalted assembly" then "trustworthy" upon his separation from them at the time of his conveying revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, it would be permissible that a report has come with it. End of quote. What is relied upon is what you have heard, and the context requires magnifying the trustworthiness, because the rebuttal of the Qur'an being a fabrication depends on the trustworthiness of the Messenger.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 22:

﴿And your companion is not a madman.﴾ He is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whom the disbelievers accuse falsely, may Allah fight them. The mention of the title "companion" (ṣuḥbah), attributed to them (i.e., "your companion"), as is the truth, is a refutation of them in the most subtle manner; for it is an indication that he (peace and blessings be upon him) grew up among you from the beginning of his affair until now, so you know him best, and that he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is the most complete of creation in intellect, the weightiest of them in speech, the most perfect of them in qualities, and the clearest of them in mind. Therefore none ascribes madness to him except one who is himself composed of foolishness and madness. Al-Zamakhshari argued from the emphasis in mentioning Gabriel (peace be upon him) and its omission in the case of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) for the superiority of Gabriel (peace be upon him) over the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). The scholars responded with what has been examined in it. The correct response, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is that the discourse is directed toward the truth of the revealed message, as evidence for the truth of what it mentions of the horrors of the Resurrection. You have learned that it is characteristic of an eloquent speaker to strip the speech down to what it is meant for, lest he consider the addition a clumsiness and an excess. There is no doubt that describing the one who brings the message as "a noble messenger" strengthens that purpose most powerfully. As for describing the one to whom it was sent, it has no place in the matter unless the purpose is to urge following him. Therefore the emphasis regarding Gabriel (peace be upon him), the enumeration of his perfect qualities, and the omission of that in the case of our Prophet, upon whom be the best of prayers and salutations, do not indicate his superiority in any way. Some of them said: the emphasis in describing Gabriel (peace be upon him) is an eloquent praise of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace); for when a king sends someone who is honored, esteemed and close to him to a person, it shows that the one to whom he is sent holds a station with him beyond which there is no station. You have learned that the context is not for emphasis in praising the one to whom it was sent. It was said: the intended meaning of "the Messenger" is our Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), just as the intended meaning of "the companion" is him, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning upon which the majority agree.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 23:

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾ That is: and by Allah, Most High, your companion, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), certainly saw the noble Messenger, Jibril (peace be upon him), upon a throne between the heaven and the earth, in the form in which Allah Most High created him, having six hundred wings. ﴿On the clear horizon﴾ And it is the highest horizon from the direction of the east, as related from al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and Sufyan. And in a report from Mujahid, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him (peace be upon him) towards the Jiyad (the region), and it is the east of Makkah.

It was said: the intended meaning is the rising point of the head of Cancer (al-Saratan), for it is the highest of the risings for the people of Makkah. And this vision occurred after the command at the Cave of Hira'. Ibn Shajarah related that it is the western horizon of the sky, but this is nothing.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the verse: he saw him in his form near Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary).

According to this view, al-Ufuq (the horizon) is said to mean "direction" (al-nahiyah), and it was said: that was called a horizon metaphorically.

﴿Wa-ma huwa﴾, that is, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿ʿala al-ghayb﴾ "upon the unseen," meaning what he reports of the revelation sent to him and of other unseen matters, ﴿bi-ḍanin﴾ "withholding," from *ḍann* (miserliness), pronounced with either a kasra or a fatḥa on the ḍād, meaning stinginess. That is, he is not a miser who withholds revelation, nor one who falls short in conveying and teaching, or in bestowing all the knowledge for which one is prepared, unlike the soothsayers (*kahana*). They reveal what they claim to know only in exchange for a payment (*ḥulwan*).

Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿA'isha, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Ibn Jubayr, ʿUrwa, Hisham ibn Jundub, Mujahid and others recited ﴿bi-ḍanin﴾ with the ḍād. Among the Seven Readers, the two grammarians (*al-Naḥwiyyan*, i.e., Ḥamza and al-Kisaʾi) and Ibn Kathir recited it as «bi-ẓanin» with the ẓāʾ, meaning "accused," from *ẓinna* (accusation, suspicion) with a kasra, which means *tuhma* (charge). This is the counterpart of the earlier description ﴿amin﴾ "trustworthy."

It has also been said that it means "weak in strength to convey the revelation," from the expression *biʾrun ẓanūn*, a well that is low in water. The first meaning is more well-known. This reading (with ẓāʾ) is preferred over the other, because it suits the context better, given the disbelievers' accusation against him (ﷺ), and clearing him of an accusation is more fitting than clearing him of stinginess. Also, the verb *tuhma* takes *ʿala* as its preposition, whereas *bukhl* does not, except when it is construed as implying a meaning such as *ḥirṣ* (eagerness).

However, al-Ṭabari said that the codices (*khuṭūṭ al-maṣahif*) all have the letter ḍād, and perhaps he meant the widely circulated codices, since they said that the codex of Ibn Masʿud has the ẓāʾ. Moreover, this does not contradict the statement of Abu ʿUbayda that in the ancient script the ḍād and the ẓāʾ do not differ except by a slight increase in the head of one of them over the other, a small difference that may cause confusion, as is well known.

As for the difference between the ḍād and the ẓāʾ in articulation (*makhraj*): the ḍād is articulated from the root of the edge of the tongue and what adjoins it of the molars, on the right or left side of the tongue, and some people are able to produce it from either side. The ẓāʾ is articulated from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper incisors.

The scholars differed over whether substituting one for the other is prohibited and invalidates the prayer (*ṣalah*) or not. It was said that it invalidates the prayer by analogy (*qiyas*), and al-Burhani reported this in *al-Muhit* from the majority of the shaykhs (*ʿammat al-mashayikh*). Al-Khulasa reported it from Abu Hanifa and Muhammad. It was also said that it does not invalidate the prayer, by juristic preference (*istiḥsan*), and al-Khulasa reported this from the majority of the shaykhs, such as Abu Muṭiʿ al-Balkhi and Muhammad ibn Salama. A group said: if it is possible to distinguish between the two, and one deliberately substitutes them in a case where the recitation was not transmitted that way, as here, and the meaning is altered, then the prayer is invalidated; otherwise it is not, because of the difficulty of distinguishing between them, especially for non-Arabs (*ʿajam*). Many of them embraced Islam in the early period, and it is not reported that the Companions urged them to make the distinction and taught it; had it been obligatory, they would have done so and it would have been transmitted. This is the position that should be adopted and issued as a legal ruling (*yuftā bihi*). Some have compiled the words whose meanings do not differ whether written with ḍād or ẓāʾ in a small treatise, and he did well in doing so. So let it be consulted, for it is important.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verses 25–26:

﴿And he is not﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿the word of an accursed devil﴾, that is: it is not the word of some of those who steal hearing (al-mustaraqah lil-sam‘, i.e., the jinn who eavesdrop on the heavens), because it is they who relay (what they overhear). This is a denial of their claim that it is soothsaying (kihanah).

﴿Then where are you going?﴾ This is a question seeking to make them lose their way regarding what they pursue concerning the matter of the Great Qur'an, like your saying to one who has left the main road and gone off into the side-paths: "Where are you going?" The fa' (then) indicates that what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it, namely the clear evidence that it is revelation (wahy).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 81, verse 27:

﴿It is not⦆ i.e., what it is ﴿but a reminder to the worlds﴾, an admonition and a great reminder for whoever has knowledge. The pronoun in "huwa" (it) also refers to the Qur'an. It is also permissible that both pronouns refer to the Messenger (ﷺ); i.e., and it is not intermixed with the word of an accursed devil, as is the case with the soothsayers (kahanah). "It is but a reminder to the worlds." His exalted saying, ﴿So where are you going?﴾ and so on, is a rebuke to them for what they pursue regarding his matter (ﷺ), and it is, as you see, [far-fetched].

[Page 62]

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿for whoever among you wills﴾ is a substitution from "the worlds," a partial substitution (badal ba'd, substitution of part for whole) from the whole. The substitute is the genitive noun, and the governing particle is repeated with it according to the well-known view. It was also said that it is the prepositional phrase (the preposition and its object). It was permitted that it be a total substitution (badal kull min kull), with the whole standing for the part, to place those who do not will in the category of beasts by way of claim, but this is far-fetched.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that he may be upright﴾ is the object of (willed), meaning: for whoever among you wills uprightness by seeking out the truth and adhering to what is correct. Its substitution from "the worlds" is because they are the ones who benefit from the reminder. ﴿And you do not will﴾, that is, uprightness through any of the means, ﴿except that God wills﴾, that is, except by God, exalted is He, willing your willing. Your willing is thus through the cause of God's willing, exalted is He. ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, the King of creation and its Nurturer, all of them. Or: you do not will uprightness with a beneficial willing that entails it, except that God wills it. So to Him, glorified is He, belongs the bounty and the truth, and He knows your uprightness if you are upright.

It was related from Sulayman ibn Musa and al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymara that when the verse ﴿for whoever among you wills that he may be upright﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said: "The matter has been left up to us: if we will, we will be upright, and if we will, we will not be upright." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And you do not will﴾, the verse. Here "an" (that) and what follows it are, as we have mentioned, in a position of genitive by the implied preposition of causation (bi'), and it was permitted that it be for accompaniment. Some scholars held that the exception is an exception from the most general of times, that is: "And you do not will uprightness at any time except the time when God, exalted is His majesty, wills your uprightness." This is based on what is reported from the Kufans concerning the permissibility of the interpretive verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb standing in for an adverb of time. In the eighth chapter of the meaning, it is said that "an" and its clause do not confer the status of a verbal noun in standing in for a time adverb. You say: "I came to you the time of the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr)," but it is not permissible to say "I came to you that you pray the afternoon prayer." The first view we mentioned is therefore preferable, and Makki took it, while al-Qadi took the second.

It has also been objected to this that "ma" (not) is for negating the present, while "an" is specific to the future; so it would follow that the time of His willing, which is future, is an adverb of time for the servant's present willing. It was answered: we do not concede that "ma" is specific to negating the present, and whoever claims its specificity to that must stipulate the absence of a contrary indication, and that absence does not hold here because of the position of "an" within its scope. Or it was answered: that "an" indicates the future is conditioned on the absence of a contrary indication, and here one exists because of what precedes it, so it is for mere verbal-nounhood. It was also said: the objection is dispelled by making the exception disjunctive (munqati'), so let it be so taken, although the basic assumption is that it is connected (muttasil), and this is not something. It has been raised in the causal sense we mentioned, something similar to this: that it would follow from "ma" being for negating the present and for the future that a later thing causes an earlier thing. The answer to this is known from what has been said, as is not hidden, so reflect on all of that. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the clearest paths.

Some of the people of ta'wil (esoteric interpretation) said: the sun is the sun of the spirit (shams al-ruh), the stars are the stars of the senses (nujum al-hawass), the mountains are the mountains of the bodily forms (jibal al-qawalib), and they move at all times, except that this becomes apparent to the veiled when the veil is lifted for him. The she-camels in calving (al-'ishar) are the bodily faculties (quwa qalibiyya), the wild beasts are the blameworthy psychic characteristics (akhlaq dhamima nafsaniyya), the seas are the seas of the natural elements ('anasir tabi'iyya), the souls are the psychic faculties (quwa nafsaniyya), and their marriage is the joining of each faculty to its work. The buried infant girl is the inspirational thoughts (khawatir ilhamiyya) that arrive upon the wayfarer, whom he buries in the grave of the body and darkens. The scrolls are on their apparent meaning. The heaven is the heaven of the breast (sama' al-sadr). The blazing fire is the fire of the soul and its kindling with the fires of desire. The Garden is the Garden of the heart. The receding stars (al-khunnas) are the lights deposited in the heart's faculties. The night is the lights of majesty (anwar jalaliyya), and the dawn is the lights of beauty (anwar jamaliyya), and so on to the end of what he said. Something is inferred from the state of one thing about another. Abu Hayyan related something of this kind and followed it with a severe rebuke, and this is only complete if the apparent meaning is denied. But if it is not denied, and what he mentioned and similar things are taken as allusion (isharah), then the matter of rebuke is not complete, as has been verified in its proper place.
